title: A Smoke-Free World Is Safer for Babies
hook: Keeping a baby away from smoke is one of the few SIDS risk factors parents fully control — and it also means fewer chest infections, ear infections, and asthma flare-ups.
key_points: Smoking in pregnancy and smoke exposure after birth both raise the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
Secondhand smoke also drives more colds, chest and ear infections, wheezing, and worse asthma in babies and children.
Make the home and car completely smoke-free — a window or another room isn't enough; smoke and residue still reach the baby.
Vaping aerosol is not a safe substitute, and 'thirdhand' residue left on clothes, hair, and surfaces carries toxins too.
content_html: Of all the things that influence a baby's safety, exposure to tobacco smoke is one of the few that's almost entirely in a family's hands. Both smoking during pregnancy and a baby breathing smoke after birth are linked to a higher risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), which is why a smoke-free environment is part of safe-sleep guidance.
extra_html: The benefits go well beyond SIDS. Babies and young children around secondhand smoke get more colds, chest infections, and ear infections, and they wheeze more — smoke is a major trigger for asthma. The protection has to be complete to work: cracking a window or stepping into the next room doesn't do it, because smoke lingers and drifts. The same goes for "thirdhand" smoke, the residue that settles into clothes, hair, upholstery, and car seats. Vaping isn't a safe workaround either — the aerosol still contains nicotine and other chemicals. The strongest step is a fully smoke-free home and car. This is general guidance; if you'd like help quitting, your doctor can point you to support that works.

related.title: Always Put a Baby to Sleep on Their Back
related.hook: Placing healthy babies on their back for every sleep — naps and night — is the single most effective step to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

related.title: A Safe Sleep Space for Baby
related.hook: Pediatric guidance for safer infant sleep is simple: a firm, flat surface with nothing in it — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.

flashcards.prompt: How is smoke exposure different from many other SIDS risk factors?

choices.text: It's something parents can fully control by keeping the baby's world smoke-free
It only matters during pregnancy, not after birth
It has no proven link to SIDS

flashcards.explanation_html: Both smoking in pregnancy and smoke exposure afterward raise SIDS risk — and unlike many factors, this one is fully within a family's control.

flashcards.prompt: Is opening a window or smoking in another room enough to protect a baby?
flashcards.back_html: No. Smoke and its residue still reach the baby. Keep the home and car completely smoke-free. Vaping aerosol isn't a safe substitute, and thirdhand residue on clothes and surfaces carries toxins too.
